sections.title: A scroll we can read only in part
sections.bodyMarkdown:
She sits between two tall pillars. On the left of the picture, a black pillar bears a white B; on the right, a white pillar bears a black J. Her blue-and-white garments flow to the ground, a white cross rests on her chest, and her crown combines curved, horn-like sides with a central disc. A yellow crescent moon lies against the lower part of her robe.

The scroll lies diagonally across her lap. It is inscribed TORA and partly covered by fabric. Behind her, a veil is patterned with pomegranates and palms, with narrow glimpses of blue at either side. The figure, pillars, and veil form a stable, frontal composition: part is available to us, while another part remains beyond view. She neither beckons nor displays the entire scroll.

[View the RWS image examined for this article](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:RWS_Tarot_02_High_Priestess.jpg)

This article uses the image to practise patient observation: allow yourself not to know yet, while noticing feelings that have not taken a clear verbal form. Intuition may suggest where a further question would help, but it still needs to be checked against evidence.

sections.title: Reading it upright
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Upright, the card can suit a moment that calls for listening, watching, or allowing information to develop. Hear someone out before answering. Notice unstated assumptions in a document. When choosing, investigate why a detail gives you pause.

Quietness need not mean inactivity. You can record observations, ask questions, hold back an uncertain judgment, and set limits on how long to wait. Her scroll reminds us that understanding what we have not read is itself a valuable kind of knowledge.

sections.title: Reading it reversed
sections.bodyMarkdown:
This reversal focuses on two possible problems: turning a strong feeling straight into a conclusion, or suppressing feelings and questions until other people cannot understand your silence. Both call for greater clarity.

Write separately what you observed, what you feel, and what you suspect might explain it. If the three are tangled together, avoid jumping to a conclusion. If the evidence is sufficient but you keep waiting, consider whether it is time to express a need or respond.

sections.title: Everyday examples
sections.bodyMarkdown:
### Something feels wrong in a meeting

Record the exact statement that gives you pause and ask about the missing condition. Turn “I have a bad feeling” into an answerable question, giving intuition a chance to produce useful information.

### Someone is replying less often

First establish what has actually changed, then ask how they are. The High Priestess cannot read their mind or turn uncertainty into proof of concealment.

### A plan is not ready to be shared

You can protect an idea while it takes shape. Still, identify who needs to know now and when a conversation would be appropriate. Making space and postponing a necessary conversation need separate attention.

articleMarkdown:
# The High Priestess — Notice what has not yet been said

II · The High Priestess · Major Arcana · RWS

**Keywords:** Observation · Intuition · Reserve

**Upright at a glance:** Be still and observe. Some information has yet to emerge.
**Reversed at a glance:** Feelings and guesses blur together, or something remains unsaid.

The High Priestess holds a scroll without fully revealing it. She draws attention to an easily overlooked fact: information can be right in front of us and still be incomplete.

## A scroll we can read only in part

She sits between two tall pillars. On the left of the picture, a black pillar bears a white B; on the right, a white pillar bears a black J. Her blue-and-white garments flow to the ground, a white cross rests on her chest, and her crown combines curved, horn-like sides with a central disc. A yellow crescent moon lies against the lower part of her robe.

The scroll lies diagonally across her lap. It is inscribed TORA and partly covered by fabric. Behind her, a veil is patterned with pomegranates and palms, with narrow glimpses of blue at either side. The figure, pillars, and veil form a stable, frontal composition: part is available to us, while another part remains beyond view. She neither beckons nor displays the entire scroll.

[View the RWS image examined for this article](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:RWS_Tarot_02_High_Priestess.jpg)

## Hidden knowledge is not evidence of someone’s secret

Waite explicitly explains the partly covered scroll as a sign that some things are spoken and others implied. He connects the veil and pillars with hidden religious knowledge and interprets the High Priestess through his own esoteric framework. “Hidden” has a historical context here; it is not an accusation that a real person is concealing something.

This article uses the image to practise patient observation: allow yourself not to know yet, while noticing feelings that have not taken a clear verbal form. Intuition may suggest where a further question would help, but it still needs to be checked against evidence.

[Read Waite’s original English discussion](https://original.sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktar02.htm)

## Reading it upright

Upright, the card can suit a moment that calls for listening, watching, or allowing information to develop. Hear someone out before answering. Notice unstated assumptions in a document. When choosing, investigate why a detail gives you pause.

Quietness need not mean inactivity. You can record observations, ask questions, hold back an uncertain judgment, and set limits on how long to wait. Her scroll reminds us that understanding what we have not read is itself a valuable kind of knowledge.

## Reading it reversed

This reversal focuses on two possible problems: turning a strong feeling straight into a conclusion, or suppressing feelings and questions until other people cannot understand your silence. Both call for greater clarity.

Write separately what you observed, what you feel, and what you suspect might explain it. If the three are tangled together, avoid jumping to a conclusion. If the evidence is sufficient but you keep waiting, consider whether it is time to express a need or respond.

## Everyday examples

### Something feels wrong in a meeting

Record the exact statement that gives you pause and ask about the missing condition. Turn “I have a bad feeling” into an answerable question, giving intuition a chance to produce useful information.

### Someone is replying less often

First establish what has actually changed, then ask how they are. The High Priestess cannot read their mind or turn uncertainty into proof of concealment.

### A plan is not ready to be shared

You can protect an idea while it takes shape. Still, identify who needs to know now and when a conversation would be appropriate. Making space and postponing a necessary conversation need separate attention.

## A short exercise

Choose an unresolved question. Write three facts, three feelings, and three guesses in separate groups, then circle one question you can check. Investigate only that question today instead of rushing to fill every gap.

## A common misreading

The High Priestess does not say that intuition is always right or that you should wait indefinitely. The pillars’ black-and-white contrast is first a feature of the image. It does not assign good and evil to two people in your life.

## Artwork and English-language sources

- [Pamela Colman Smith, The High Priestess, RWS Pam-A](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:RWS_Tarot_02_High_Priestess.jpg)
- [A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot, Part II, II. The High Priestess (1911 transcription)](https://original.sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktar02.htm)
- [A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot, Part III §3, The Greater Arcana and Their Divinatory Meanings (1911 transcription)](https://original.sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pkt0303.htm)

Each image was individually inspected. The English source is the transcription labelled 1911; the artwork is the Pam-A scan identified on Commons. Sources checked: 2026-10-07.

The upright and reversed interpretations, examples, and exercises are original material for reflection, not line-by-line translations of old divinatory lists. Tarot cannot establish future events, another person’s thoughts, or a health condition.

sourceRecord.title: 女祭司 看见还没有说出的部分
sourceRecord.uprightQuickTake: 先静下来观察，有些信息还没浮出来
sourceRecord.reversedQuickTake: 感觉和猜测混在一起，或有话一直没说
sourceRecord.hook: 女祭司把卷轴拿在手里，却没有完全展开。她让人注意到一个容易忽略的事实：信息就在眼前，也可能仍不完整。
imageReading: 她端坐在两根高柱之间。画面左边是带有白色 B 字母的黑柱，右边是带有黑色 J 字母的白柱。蓝白色衣袍垂落到地面，胸前有白色十字，头冠由两侧弯曲的角状形体和中间圆盘组成。黄色新月靠在袍子下方。
卷轴斜放在膝前，写有 TORA，部分被衣料遮住。身后帷幕布满石榴与棕榈纹样，两侧窄隙透出蓝色背景。人物、双柱和帷幕构成稳定的正面构图：我们被允许看见一部分，又被挡在另一部分之外。她没有伸手招呼，也没有展示卷轴的全部内容。
tradition: Waite 明确把卷轴的半遮半露解释为有些内容被说出，有些只被暗示。他将帷幕、双柱与隐秘宗教知识联系起来，并用自己的神秘学体系阐释女祭司。这里的“隐秘”有历史语境，不是对现实中某个人藏有秘密的指控。
本篇借这个画面练习耐心观察：允许自己暂时不知道，同时留意还没有形成完整语言的感受。直觉可以提示哪里值得多问一句，但它仍需要与现实证据相互核对。
uprightMeaning: 正位常适合放在需要听、看、等待资料成熟的时刻。有人说话时，先听完再回应；读一份材料时，留意没有交代的前提；做选择时，辨认自己为什么对某个细节迟疑。
安静并不意味着什么都不做。你可以记录、提问、保留尚未确定的判断，并给等待一个范围。她的卷轴提醒我们，知道自己没读到什么，也是一种重要的理解。
reversedMeaning: 本篇的逆位着重检查两种偏差：把强烈感觉直接当结论，或压住自己的感受和问题，直到别人无法理解你的沉默。两种情况都需要让模糊的东西更清楚。
可以分别写下“我看到的事实”“我的感受”“我猜测的原因”。若三栏混在一起，就先不要下定论；若事实已足够而你仍一直等待，也要考虑是否该说出需要或作出回应。

situations.title: 会议上觉得哪里不对
situations.text: 记录让你迟疑的具体句子，问清缺少的条件。把“我有不好的预感”转成可以回答的问题，直觉才有机会带来有用信息。

situations.title: 对方最近回复变少
situations.text: 先确认实际变化，再询问近况。女祭司不能让你读到对方的内心，也不能把不确定自动变成隐瞒。

situations.title: 还不想公开一个计划
situations.text: 可以先保护尚未成形的想法，但明确哪些人现在需要知道、何时适合沟通。保留空间与拖延必要对话，需要分别处理。

sourceRecord.practice: 选一个未确定的问题，把事实、感受、猜测各写三条，再圈出一个可以核实的疑问。今天只去核实它，不急着填满所有空白。
sourceRecord.commonMisread: 女祭司不是“你的直觉永远正确”，也不是让你无限等待的理由。双柱的黑白首先是画面中的对照，不能直接给现实中的两个人分配善恶。
sourceRecord.sourceClaim: 黑白双柱及字母；Tora卷轴半遮及其“已说出/被暗示”解释；帷幕棕榈与石榴。事实感受猜测练习为原创。
sourceRecord.readingApproach: 图像细读、Waite历史解释与原创现代反思分别标示；正逆位是学习与自我反思提示，不用来确认未来、健康或他人隐秘行为。
sourceRecord.reverseMethod: 当代反思式读法，依据正位主题的受阻、失衡或尚待整合展开；不是对Waite旧逆位词条逐项翻译。
